name: Turanism
summary: Turanism is the nationalist idea that the Turkic peoples, and in its Hungarian and Finnish strands the supposed Ural-Altaic kin, share an ancestral homeland (Turan) and should be united culturally and, in the long run, politically. Its Turkish mainstream, shaped by Ziya Gökalp, defines the nation by shared language and culture, wants a modern national state with secular law, a protected national economy and a solidarist order between classes, and treats Turan as a distant ideal. Racial, expansionist and militarist versions appeared in its later and Hungarian forms.
scope: Turanism as the defining sources frame it: the movement to unite the Turkic, and in its wider form the Ural-Altaic (Turkish, Mongolian, Finno-Ugric), peoples culturally and, as a distant ideal, politically (Britannica, Pekesen). Its mainstream is the Turkish strand of Ziya Gökalp, who made Turan a popular ideal and then narrowed it to a cultural union of Turks (TDV, Atatürk Dergisi); the Hungarian strand (Vámbéry, Turan Society) is the main parallel. Principles of Turkism is Gökalp's own text, tied through him as key figure. It excludes Nihal Atsız's racial Turanism (reserved to Atsizism) and Pan-Turkism as a separate ideology; answers on issues Gökalp never treated stay unanswered.

missingStatements.text: Peoples who share a language family and ancestry should work toward political unity across existing borders.
missingStatements.rationale: Turan, the union of kin peoples, is the movement's defining aim, stated by Gökalp as the ultimate ideal of Turkism and by Hungarian Turanists as kinship with the East.

missingStatements.text: A nation's language should be purified of foreign words and its older vocabulary revived.
missingStatements.rationale: Gökalp's Linguistic Turkism is a core programme item calling for replacing Arabic and Persian borrowings with old Turkish words.
missingStatements.declined: Linguistic purism is narrow to Turkish language reform; revive-national-language covers the nearby question.

missingStatements.text: A nation's tradition is better represented by its pre-religious ancestral past than by its recent history.
missingStatements.rationale: Gökalp and Turanists draw on pre-Islamic Turkic khanates, the Sky God religion and Orkhon inscriptions as the authentic national culture and Red Apple memory.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow to national-origin myths of Turkism; no common axis other ideologies could take a side on.

notes: Gökalp himself narrowed Turan to Turkic peoples and called it a long-term cultural ideal, and the Turkish Republic rejected pan-Turkism; Hungarian Turanism was more racial and Trianon-driven and Atsiz's strand was racist, so answers on race, expansion and authoritarianism differ by strand. Gökalp's own quoted lines stress language, culture and religion over race. Later pass 2026-11-24: answers resting on Wikipedia articles (Turanism, Pan-Turkism, Ziya Gökalp) were nulled or re-based on Gökalp's Principles of Turkism, Britannica, Pekesen (IEG) and the TDV entry; the Wikipedia pages stay listed only for the answer histories that cite them. Themes searched in the Principles: marriage and family law, nationality, language, religion, labour and guilds, party and state, citizenship.

keyFigures.quote: Gökalp, who is still considered by some circles as a racist or irredentist, always remained at a distance from racial and biological characteristics even during the period when he was known as a Turanist.
keyFigures.role: Thinker who made Turan a popular ideal, then narrowed it to a cultural Turkish nation

keyFigures.quote: The Hungarian Turkologist Armin Vámbéry (Hermann Wamberger, 1832‒1913) is regarded as the "pioneer" of the Pan-Turkist and Turanist currents.
keyFigures.role: Hungarian Turkologist, pioneer of the Turanist current

keyFigures.quote: The Finnish philologist and ethnologist Matthias Alexander Castrén (1813‒1852) , who dealt with the Ural, Altaic and Paleo-Siberian languages, postulated a linguistic, cultural, and racial unity of the so-called Ural-Altaic peoples.
keyFigures.role: Finnish philologist who postulated Ural-Altaic unity
